title: Starts of Lessons, Problems and Solutions https://curriculumteamleader.wordpress.com/2024/06/11/starts-of-lessons-problems-and-solutions/
author: Peter Foster
summary: Pete Foster catalogues three recurring problems at the start of lessons -- slow engagement with the first task, student lateness, and slow resource collection -- with concrete, scripted solutions for each. For slow starts, he recommends diagnosing the root cause first, then clearly defined expectations delivered via consistent phrasing, narrated countdowns, and active circulation to catch non-completion rather than only checking later in the lesson. For lateness, he advises calm, brief acknowledgment of the consequence without engaging in a disruptive argument, plus a clear decision in advance about what late students will complete for the starter task. For slow resource collection, he recommends removing student responsibility where possible by pre-distributing books before the lesson. Throughout, he stresses that these solutions only work with consistency and a school behaviour system that actually backs up sanctions.
points: Foster's core prescription for slow starters: define the expectation with consistent phrasing and a narrated countdown, then actually circulate to check completion rather than assuming compliance.
For late arrivals, he recommends a calm, brief acknowledgment of the consequence rather than an in-the-moment argument that disrupts the rest of the class.
He pre-decides what late students will complete rather than letting them simply wait for the lesson to start, weighing trade-offs between focusing on recent content versus easier early questions.

For resource collection, his default is to remove the responsibility from students altogether by pre-distributing books before the lesson, reserving an explicitly taught passing-down-rows routine for contexts where that isn't feasible.
quotes: Starts of lessons set the tone for what follows. But there is potential for various problems in this part of the lesson.
Teachers who are generally good at circulating and checking during the lesson sometimes miss non-completion in the starter (I’m talking about myself as much as anyone else).
There’s tension between sanctioning the late student and getting into an argument or conversation that is going to disrupt the lesson.
It’s better to give a clear expectation that they will complete something than just to let them write the title/date and wait for the lesson to start.
The above should work if you are consistent and firm and your school has a system that sanctions lateness in some way.
